Sri Santosh Kumar Singh, learned counsel for the petitioner has sought
100→to challenge the order by contending that since the Executive Engineer, who is
the assessing officer did not make the inspection of the premises himself, and
the same  was done by the Junior Engineer, the order of provisional assessment
is invalid. To support his submission, learned counsel for the petitioner places
reliance upon the decision of the Supreme Court in Executive Engineer Vs.
M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill3.
4.
Sri Devendra Kumar Tiwari, learned Additional Chief Standing Counsel
has appeared for the State respondents.
5. 
110→Sri Sushil Kumar Pandey, learned counsel who appears on behalf of
respondent nos.2 to 4, does not dispute the fact that the inspection of the
premises was made by the Junior Engineer. He however, submits that the order
of provisional assessment having been made by the Executive Engineer, who is
the assessing officer, the said order cannot be said to be bad in law.
6. 
The Supreme Court in the case of M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill (supra),
1
2003 Act
2
120→Code 2005
3   (2012) 2 SCC 108

4
while examining the ambit and scope of powers of assessment under Section
126 of the 2003 Act, observed that the provisions of Section 126, read with
Section 127 of 2003 Act, are a code in themselves and that the purpose of
Section 126 is to put restriction on unauthorized consumption of electricity.
The observations made in the judgment in this regard are as follows:
“16. 
130→First and foremost, we have to examine how provisions like
Section 126 of the 2003 Act should be construed. From the objects and
reasons stated by us in the beginning of this judgment, it is clear that
`revenue focus' was one of the principal considerations that weighed
with the Legislature while enacting this law. The regulatory regime
under the 2003 Act empowers the Commission to frame the tariff,
which shall be the very basis for raising a demand upon a consumer,
depending upon the category to which such consumer belongs and the
purpose for which the power is sanctioned to such consumer. ...
18. … The provisions of Section 126, read with Section 127 of the
140→2003 Act, in fact, becomes a code in themselves. Right from the
initiation of the proceedings by conducting an inspection, to the right
to file an appeal before the appellate authority, all matters are squarely
covered under these provisions. It specifically provides the method of
computation of the amount that a consumer would be liable to pay for
excessive consumption of the electricity and for the manner of
conducting assessment proceedings. In other words, Section 126 of the
2003 Act has a purpose to achieve, i.e., to put an implied restriction on
such unauthorized consumption of electricity.
19.
150→The provisions of the 2003 Act, applicable regulations and the
Agreement executed between the parties at the time of sanction of the
load prohibit consumption of electricity in excess of maximum
sanctioned/ installed load. In the event of default, it also provides for
the consequences that a consumer is likely to face. It embodies
complete process for assessment, determination and passing of a
demand order. This defined legislative purpose cannot be permitted to
be frustrated by interpreting a provision in a manner not intended in
law. This Court would have to apply the principle of purposive
interpretation in preference to textual interpretation of the provisions
160→of Section 126 of the 2003 Act.”
7.
It was further stated as follows:
36.
…
The provisions of Section 126 contemplate the following steps
to be taken :
(i) An assessing officer is to conduct inspection of a place or premises
and the equipments, gadgets, machines, devices found connected or
used in such place.
170→(ii) The formation of a conclusion that such person has indulged in
unauthorized use of electricity.
(iii) The assessing officer to provisionally assess, to the best of his
judgment, the electricity charges payable by such person.

5
(iv) The order of provisional assessment to be served upon the person
concerned in the manner prescribed, giving him an opportunity to file
objections, if any, against the provisional assessment.
(v) The assessing officer has to afford a reasonable opportunity of
180→being heard to such person and pass a final order of assessment within
30 days from the date of service of such order of provisional
assessment.
(vi) The person, upon whom the provisional order of assessment is
served, is at liberty to pay the said amount within seven days of the
receipt of such order and where he files such objections, final order of
assessment shall be passed, against which such person has a right of
appeal under Section 127 of the 2003 Act within the prescribed period
of limitation.” 
8. The aforesaid observations indicate that the assessment proceedings are to
190→commence with the inspection of the premises by an assessing officer resulting
in formation of a conclusion that there has been an unauthorized use of
electricity, and thereafter assessing officer is to provisionally assess, to the best
of his judgment, the electricity charges payable by such consumer as well as to
pass a provisional order under Section 126 (2) of the 2003 Act. The officer is
also obliged to serve a notice in terms of Section 126 (3) upon any such
consumer, requiring him to file his objection, if any, against the provisional
assessment before final order of assessment is passed within thirty days from
the date of such order of provisional assessment. The person served with the
order of provisional assessment may accept such assessment and deposit the
200→amount with the officer within seven days of service of such provisional
assessment order upon him, or prefer an appeal against final assessment under
Section 127 of the 2003 Act.
9. 
The order of provisional assessment, in the present case, having been
passed by the Executive Engineer, based on inspection report of the Junior
Engineer, the contention of the petitioner seeking to assail its validity, cannot
be said to be without basis.
10.
The question with regard to the maintainability and scope of interference
210→in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution despite availability of an
alternative remedy under Section 127 of 2003 Act, was also examined in the
case of M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill (supra), and it was held that availability of

6
alternative remedy although not absolute bar to exercise of writ jurisdiction, the
High Court would exercise this jurisdiction with circumspection in exceptional
cases depending upon the facts and circumstances of the case. The observations
made in this regard are as follows:
“78.
220→Once the order of assessment is finally passed and is served
upon the consumer, he is expected to pay the said charges unless, being
aggrieved from such an order, he prefers an appeal under Section 127
of the 2003 Act. The appeal under Section 127 would lie only against
the final order passed under Section 126 that too within 30 days of the
said order. The appeal shall be filed, maintained and dealt with in
accordance with the procedure specified in Section 127 of the 2003
Act. A bare reading of the provisions of Section 127 shows that it is the
final order made under Section 126 which is appealable under Section
127 of the 2003 Act. In other words, issuance of a notice or a
230→provisional order of assessment as may be made by the assessing
officer in terms of sub-section (1) to sub-section (3) of Section 126 of
the 2003 Act would not be the order against which an appeal would lie.
79.
It may be noticed that admittedly the present respondent had
not preferred any appeal against the provisional order of assessment
dated 25th July, 2009 and, in fact, had preferred a writ petition against
the very issuance of a notice issued in terms of Sub-sections (2) and (3)
of Section 126 of the 2003 Act. This brings us to the question as to
what is the scope of jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution
240→of India in the face of the provisions of Section 127 of the 2003 Act.
80.
It is a settled canon of law that the High Court would not
normally interfere in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of
the Constitution of India where statutory alternative remedy is
available. It is equally settled that this canon of law is not free of
exceptions. The courts, including this Court, have taken the view that
the statutory remedy, if provided under a specific law, would impliedly
oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts. The High Court in exercise of
its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of
250→India can entertain writ or appropriate proceedings despite availability
of an alternative remedy. This jurisdiction, the High Court would
exercise with some circumspection in exceptional cases, particularly,
where the cases involve a pure question of law or vires of an Act are
challenged. This class of cases we are mentioning by way of
illustration and should not be understood to be an exhaustive
exposition of law which, in our opinion, is neither practical nor
possible to state with precision. The availability of alternative statutory
or other remedy by itself may not operate as an absolute bar for
exercise of jurisdiction by the Courts. It will normally depend upon the
260→facts and circumstances of a given case. The further question that
would inevitably come up for consideration before the Court even in
such cases would be as to what extent the jurisdiction has to be
exercised.
81.
Should the Courts determine on merits of the case or should it
preferably answer the preliminary issue or jurisdictional issue arising
in the facts of the case and remit the matter for consideration on merits
by the competent authority? Again, it is somewhat difficult to state

270→7
with absolute clarity any principle governing such exercise of
jurisdiction. It always will depend upon the facts of a given case. We
are of the considered view that interest of administration of justice
shall be better sub-served if the cases of the present kind are heard by
the courts only where it involves primary questions of jurisdiction or
the matters which goes to the very root of jurisdiction and where the
authorities have acted beyond the provisions of the Act. However, it
should only be for the specialized Tribunal or the appellate authorities
to examine the merits of assessment or even factual matrix of the
280→case.”
11.
In the case of M/s Sri Seetaram Rice Mill (supra), the consumer did not
file objection/reply to the provisional assessment, but challenged the same
before the High Court by filing a writ petition on grounds of lack of authority
and jurisdiction on the part of Executive Engineer to frame the provisional
assessment by alleging unauthorized use of electricity.
12.
The Supreme Court, while answering the question of maintainability of
the writ petition, held that the High Court did not fall in error of jurisdiction in
290→entertaining the writ petition, but certainly failed to finally exercise the
jurisdiction within the prescribed limitations of law for exercise of such
jurisdiction. It was observed that it would have been proper exercise of
jurisdiction, if the High Court, upon entertaining and deciding the writ petition
on a jurisdictional issue, would have remanded the matter to the competent
authority for its adjudication on merits and in accordance with law. It was
stated as follows:
86.
In the present case, the High Court did not fall in error of
jurisdiction in entertaining the writ petition but certainly failed to finally
300→exercise the jurisdiction within the prescribed limitations of law for
exercise of such jurisdiction. Keeping in view the functions and
expertise of the specialized body constituted under the Act including the
assessing officer, it would have been proper exercise of jurisdiction, if
the High Court, upon entertaining and deciding the writ petition on a
jurisdictional issue, would have remanded the matter to the competent
authority for its adjudication on merits and in accordance with law. In
the facts of the present case, the High Court should have answered the
question of law relating to lack of jurisdiction and exercise of
jurisdiction in futility without travelling into and determining the
310→validity of the demand which squarely fell within the domain of the
specialized authority. The High Court should have remanded the case to
the assessing officer with a direction to the respondent to file its
objections including non-applicability of the tariff before the assessing
authority and for determination in accordance with law.”
13.
The observations made in this regard in the judgment of M/s Sri

8
Seetaram Rice Mill (supra), in its concluding paragraphs, may also be
320→gainfully reproduced:
87.
Having dealt with and answered determinatively the questions
framed in the judgment, we consider it necessary to precisely record the
conclusions of our judgment which are as follows:- 
… … ...
5.
The High Court did not commit any error of jurisdiction
in entertaining the writ petition against the order raising a
jurisdictional challenge to the notice/provisional assessment
330→order dated 25th July, 2009. However, the High Court
transgressed its jurisdictional limitations while travelling into the
exclusive domain of the Assessing Officer relating to passing of
an order of assessment and determining factual controversy of
the case. 
6.
The High Court having dealt with the jurisdictional issue,
the appropriate course of action would have been to remand the
matter to the Assessing Authority by directing the consumer to
file his objections, if any, as contemplated under Section 126(3)
340→and require the Authority to pass a final order of assessment as
contemplated under Section 126(5) of the 2003 Act in
accordance with law. 
88.
For the reasons afore-recorded, the judgment of the High Court
is set aside and the matter is remanded to the Assessing Officer to pass a
final order of assessment expeditiously, after providing opportunity to
the respondent herein to file objections, if any, to the provisional
assessment order, as contemplated under Section 126(3) of the 2003
Act.” 
350→14.
The sole ground, which has been urged before us to challenge the order
of provisional assessment, is that the said order passed by the assessing officer
is based on an inspection report of some other authority. It is for the said reason
that we have been persuaded to entertain the writ petition despite considerable
delay and laches in raising the challenge to the provisional assessment order
dated 27th July, 2024, and the entitlement of the consumer to file objections
against the provisional assessment, and also of opportunity of availing hearing
before a final order of assessment is made, which in turn, would be subject to a
statutory remedy of appeal under Section 127 of the 2003 Act.
360→15.
Counsel for the petitioner has not addressed us on the merits of the case
apart from making his submissions on the point of procedural infirmity in the
order of provisional assessment.
16.
We may also record that we have not examined the case on its merits on

9
the sufficiency of the material available on record which formed the basis of
the order of provisional assessment. That, in our view, would be within the
370→domain of the assessing officer while exercising the statutory powers under
Section 126 of 2003 Act.
17.
The fact regarding lodging of the FIR for theft of electricity under
Section 135 of 2003 Act is undisputed. It is also not disputed that it is after
lodging of the aforesaid report that the proceedings for assessment for
unauthorized use of electricity under Section 126 of 2003 Act have been
initiated.
18.
The provisions of Section 126, read with Section 127 of 2003 Act, have
380→been held to be a complete code in matters relating to assessment in a case
where there is an allegation of unauthorized use of electricity. From the stage
of initiation of proceedings by conducting an inspection to determination and
passing of a final order of assessment, it embodies a complete process.
19. The provisional assessment order has been passed by the Executive
Engineer exercising powers of the assessing officer conferred under Section
126 of the 2003 Act. It is not the case of the petitioner that it suffers from any
jurisdictional error; rather the order has been assailed on the ground of having
been passed without following the correct process, resulting in a procedural
error.
390→20.
This Court having been persuaded to entertain the writ petition assailing
the order of provisional assessment on the ground of procedural infirmity,
would yet have to be mindful that it is only for the specialized authority to
examine merits of assessment and the factual matrix of the case.
21.
We may observe that, as a general principle, where an order is set aside
due to procedural infirmities or non-adherence to statutory procedure, the Court
exercising powers of judicial review, would require the matter to be remanded
to the competent authority for proper adjudication. This would also be
400→necessary to ensure that all legal requirements are met and justice is done to the

10
parties without any prejudice caused by infraction of any procedural
requirement.
22.
The impugned order of provisional assessment is, therefore, set aside on
the ground that the same is not based on the inspection made by the assessing
officer, and the matter is remanded to respondent no.3-assessing officer, to
initiate proceedings for assessment under Section 126 of 2003 Act, afresh, in
410→accordance with the procedure under law. 
23.
With the aforesaid observations, the writ petition is disposed of.
